Abstract— Deploying depth estimation networks in the real
world requires high-level robustness against various adverse
conditions to ensure safe and reliable autonomy. For this
purpose, many autonomous vehicles employ multi-modal sensor
systems, including an RGB camera, NIR camera, thermal
camera, LiDAR, or Radar. They mainly adopt two strategies
to use multiple sensors: modality-wise and multi-modal fused
inference. The former method is flexible but memory-inefficient,
unreliable, and vulnerable. Multi-modal fusion can provide
high-level reliability, yet it needs a specialized architecture.
In this paper, we propose an effective solution, named alignand-fuse strategy, for the depth estimation from multi-spectral
images. In the align stage, we align embedding spaces between
multiple spectrum bands to learn shareable representation
across multi-spectral images by minimizing contrastive loss of
global and spatially aligned local features with geometry cue.
After that, in the fuse stage, we train an attachable feature
fusion module that can selectively aggregate the multi-spectral
features for reliable and robust prediction results. Based on
the proposed method, a single-depth network can achieve both
spectral-invariant and multi-spectral fused depth estimation
while preserving reliability, memory efficiency, and flexibility.
I. INTRODUCTION
Reliable and precise spatial understanding is the most
fundamental prior condition for level 5 autonomous driving
against adverse weather and lighting conditions, such as rain,
fog, dust, haze, and low-light environments. Therefore, numerous autonomous vehicle platforms [1]–[5] concurrently
perform perception tasks from multi-modal inputs (e.g., RGB
camera, thermal camera, LiDAR, and Radar). Usually, they
employ two main strategies to exploit multiple modality
sensors: modality-wise and modality-fused inference [1], [2],
[6]. The former conducts a target task independently with
each modality input. Therefore, it has high-level flexibility
that doesn’t tie in with other modality inputs, yet robustness
and reliability are not ensured. The latter can achieve highlevel robustness, reliability, and performance. However, it
suffers from an alignment problem between sensors, the need
for fusion-oriented architecture, and low flexibility tied with
other modality inputs.
arXiv:2503.00793v1  [cs.CV]  2 Mar 2025

Furthermore, modern perception tasks mostly deploy a
deep neural network and data-driven machine learning technique to achieve high-level accuracy. The two problems arise
between multi-model sensors: 1) the domain gap between
each modality and 2) the absence of general representation.
Usually, most neural networks are designed for each modality
and don’t consider generalization ability across other heterogeneous modalities. Also, some specific modality (e.g.,
RGB image) gets high-level performance boosting based
on a large-scale dataset pre-trained backbone network by
leveraging learned general representation. On the other hand,
non-conventional sensors (e.g., NIR and thermal images)
cannot leverage the general feature representation of a pretrained backbone network due to the absence of large-scale
datasets.
Therefore, we need effective solutions for domain generalization across multi-modal sensors and un-constrained
multi-sensor fusion while achieving high-level flexibility,
performance, robustness, and reliability. To this end, in this
paper, we propose a multi-spectral generalization method for
the monocular depth estimation task and an attachable fusion
module that can boost performance while not degrading the
learned generalization ability. Our proposed method can be
applied to common monocular depth estimation networks,
and the trained network can infer a depth map from both
single-modal input and multi-modal input. Our contributions
are summarized as follows:
• We propose a multi-spectral generalization method that
learns a shared representation across multi-spectral feature spaces by minimizing contrastive losses of multispectral global features and spatially aligned local features for spectral-invariant monocular depth estimation.
• We propose an attachable fusion module that can adaptively aggregate multi-spectral features by preserving
reliable features and suppressing suspicious features
based on a spectral-shared feature consistency.
• We validate that our proposed method can be applied
to common monocular depth networks (e.g., MiDaS
and NeWCRF) and shows high-level robustness and
performance in various sensors and test environments.
II. RELATED WORKS
A. Deep Monocular Depth Estimation
Visible Spectral Band. Most standard network architectures for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) have been proposed for the visible spectral band. The taxonomy of MDE
networks is roughly categorized into the methods utilizing
per-pixel regression [7]–[10], per-pixel classification [11],
[12], and classification-and-regression [13], [14] head. The
networks utilize convolution layer [7], [8], [12] and transformer block [10], [13]–[15] to project input image into
non-linear feature space. After that, the projected features
are mapped to a depth map via their prediction head (e.g.,
regression, classification, or combined heads).
Thermal Spectral Band. The thermal spectral band
can provide high-level robustness against various adverse
weather and lighting conditions, such as rain, fog, dust,
haze, and low-light conditions. However, different from the
visible spectral band, the deep MDE task for the thermal
image has been relatively less studied. Recently, a few
works [16]–[21] have been proposed in the self-supervised
MDE field. They mainly utilize extra modality information to
train the MDE network for thermal images, such as aligned
RGB images [16], [18], image translation network [17], and
adversarial learning [20], [21] between RGB and thermal
images. On the other hand, the research [19] trains an MDE
network only with a thermal video.
B. Depth Estimation from Multi-sensor Fusion
Multi-sensor fusion is a fundamental way to achieve
robustness and higher performance for various computer
vision and robotics applications. The most widely used
sensors for depth estimation are a RGB camera, LiDAR,
and Radar. Therefore, numerous RGB-Lidar and RGB-Radar
fusion researches for depth estimation [22]–[29] have been
proposed, known as the depth completion task. Also, a
few RGB-NIR and thermal-LiDAR fusion methods [30]–
[33] have been proposed for a robust solution against lowlight and adverse weather conditions. However, these lines
of solutions are designed for sensor fusion purposes, so they
need a specialized network architecture.
III. PROPOSED METHOD: ALIGN-AND-FUSE STRATEGY

multi-modal input (i.e., RGB, NIR, and thermal image). To
this end, we proposed a two-stage training method, named
”Align-and-Fuse,” as shown in Fig. 2.

multi-spectrum domains for spectral-invariant depth estimation. More specifically, we divide each latent feature of multispectral images into spectral-shared and spectral-specific
features. After that, we minimize contrastive losses of global
and spatially aligned local features of multi-spectral images
to make spectral-shared and spectral-specific feature spaces.

C. Fuse Stage: Selective Multi-spectrum Fusion
1) Attention Mask for Reliable Feature Selection: After
completing align stage training, we conduct fusion stage to
train the multi-spectral feature fusion module. Each modality

and robustness may vary for given lighting and weather

structure details, yet this information is unreliable in lowlight conditions. Therefore, it is necessary to suppress the

For this purpose, we exploit cross-spectral shared embedding space that is formed in align stage. After the

The overall training objective is a combination of the align

E. Implementation Details
We implement the align stage and the fuse stage in two
different stages during the training process. The first stage
aligns the multi-spectral feature space through contrastive
learning, and the second stage fuses the multi-spectral features
through the attachable fusion module. The model architecture
is based on the MiDaS network [39], which is a popular
monocular depth estimation network. We use the PyTorch
framework for implementation and train on CUDA-enabled
GPUs with mixed-precision training. The training data
is synthesized from various sensor inputs, including RGB,
NIR, and thermal images, each with different spatial resolutions
and noise levels. The network is trained for 1000
iterations with a batch size of 64. The learning rate is
set to 2e-4 for the first 500 iterations and then decaying
to 2e-5 for the remaining 500 iterations. The contrastive
loss is weighted with a coefficient of 1.0, and the geometric
consistency loss is set to 0.1.
F. Performance Metrics
We evaluate the performance of our method using standard
depth estimation metrics, including Root Mean Squared
Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and
Disparity PSNR. Additionally, we evaluate the robustness
against different environmental conditions, such as varying
lighting, rain, and fog.

III. PROPOSED METHOD: ALIGN-AND-FUSE STRATEGY

A. Method Overview
Our proposed method trains and extends an off-the-shelf network to infer a depth map from both single and multi-modal inputs. The method consists of two stages: the align stage and the fuse stage.

Align Stage: The network learns a shared representation across multi-spectral images by minimizing contrastive losses of global and local features. The alignment process uses inverse warping to project features into a common spatial coordinate system.

Fuse Stage: After the alignment stage, the network estimates a reliable and robust depth map by selectively aggregating multi-spectral features using a masked attention mechanism and a transformer-based fusion module. The geometric consistency loss is applied to ensure that the depth maps from different modalities maintain consistent geometric information.

B. Align Stage: Multi-spectrum Generalization
1) Spatial Feature Alignment: Each multi-spectral image is projected into the same spatial coordinate system using inverse warping. This allows the network to extract features that are aligned across different sensors.

2) Latent Alignment via Contrastive Learning: The network divides each feature map into spectral-shared and spectral-specific components. Global contrastive loss encourages similar global features across different spectra, while local contrastive loss ensures that local features are consistent across the same spectrum.

C. Fuse Stage: Selective Multi-spectral Fusion
1) Attention Mask for Reliable Feature Selection: The network computes an attention mask based on the similarity of shared features from different spectra. Unreliable features are suppressed based on this mask.

2) Weighted Feature Aggregation: The multi-spectral features are weighted according to the attention mask and then fused using a transformer-based module.

3) Geometric Consistency Loss: The fused features are enforced to maintain geometric consistency across different spectral bands.
